lesson.topicTitle: 1. Structure, Bonding & Introduction to Organic Chemistry

specAnchors.text: understand the meaning of the term ‘electronegativity’ as applied to atoms in a covalent bond

be able to distinguish between polar bonds and polar molecules and predict whether or not a given molecule is likely to be polar Further suggested practical Determine the effect of an electrostatic force on jets of liquids (water, ethanol and cyclohexane) and use the results to determine whether the molecules are polar or non-polar

primer.text: Electronegativity scores an atom's pull on a bonded pair - fluorine 4.0 tops the Pauling scale - and the difference between two atoms decides everything: matched pulls share fairly, the 0.3-1.7 band polarises the bond with delta charges, and differences above about 2 split into ions. This note closes with whole-molecule polarity: CH3Cl polar, CCl4 cancelled.

modules.title: The power to pull a pair
modules.opening: Electronegativity is an atom's power to attract the shared pair of a covalent bond toward itself. Wherever two bonded atoms differ in this power, the electron distribution turns unsymmetrical, because each nucleus tugs on the outer-shell electrons in proportion to its pull. The Pauling scale numbers the tug, and fluorine tops the whole table at 4.0.
keyPoints: An atom's electronegativity is its power, inside a covalent bond, to draw the shared electron pair toward itself.
Different electronegativities in a bond make the electron distribution unsymmetrical.
The effect arises from the positive nucleus attracting outer-shell electrons toward itself.
The Pauling scale assigns each atom an electronegativity value.
Fluorine is the most electronegative element, valued at 4.0 on the Pauling scale.

low.restatement: In a bond between two different atoms, the greedier nucleus pulls the shared pair closer; the Pauling scale scores that greediness, with fluorine the greediest of all.
low.analogy: Two friends sharing fries: the hungrier one's end of the tray always ends up fuller.
low.examPointer: Quoting the definition - power over the bonded electron pair, inside a covalent bond - is the quotable mark.

medium.restatement: Electronegativity quantifies nuclear pull per bonding electron: when the two nuclei's pulls differ, electron density shifts toward the stronger one, and the Pauling scale - fluorine at 4.0 at the top - provides the comparative numbers.
medium.analogy: Two magnets of different strength holding the same paperclip: the clip rests nearer the stronger magnet.
medium.examPointer: When comparing elements, cite the Pauling values - 'fluorine, 4.0' beats 'fluorine, very high'.

modules.title: Difference decides the bond
modules.opening: Electronegativity difference is the referee between bonding types. Similar pulls share fairly and stay covalent; very different pulls tear the pair into ions - a Pauling gap of two or more tips into ionic territory, and above 1.7 ions form. Between 0.3 and 1.7 the bond stays covalent but polar, with the pair drawn toward the stronger atom and delta charges appearing at the two ends.
keyPoints: Large electronegativity differences tend to form ionic bonds; similar values form covalent bonds.
Intermediate differences between covalently bonded atoms produce polar bonds.
A Pauling difference of 2 or more leads to ionic bonding; less than 2 leads to covalent bonding.
Differences of 0.3 to 1.7 give polar covalent bonds with electrons drawn to the more electronegative atom.
Polar bonds separate the charge centres: delta-negative on the stronger atom, delta-positive on the weaker.

low.restatement: Matched pulls share fairly (pure covalent), mismatched pulls share unevenly (polar covalent), and wildly mismatched pulls stop sharing altogether (ionic).
low.analogy: Splitting a bill between equals, between a big earner and a small one, or simply handing the whole bill to the rich friend - three sharing regimes.
low.examPointer: Learn the bands: 0.3 to 1.7 polar covalent, above 1.7 ionic, and the round rule of 2 or more for full ionic character.

medium.restatement: The electronegativity difference interpolates a continuum: zero difference gives a nonpolar covalent bond, the 0.3-1.7 band gives polar covalent bonds with separated charge centres, and beyond about 1.7 to 2 the pair transfers outright, making ions.
medium.analogy: A dimmer switch between pure sharing (off) and full transfer (on): the difference slider sets the polarity at every setting between.
medium.examPointer: Assign delta signs by direction: the more electronegative atom always takes delta-negative.

modules.title: Dipoles and the whole molecule
modules.opening: A polar bond earns a dipole moment - the measure of its polarity - drawn as an arrow pointing at the delta-negative end. Whole molecules need a second look: add up each bond's polarity, then ask how the bonds sit in space. CH3Cl's dipoles leave a net pull toward chlorine, so it is polar; CCl4's four identical dipoles cancel by symmetry, so it is not.
keyPoints: The dipole moment measures how polar a bond is.
The dipole arrow points to the partially negative end of the dipole.
Judging molecular polarity needs each bond's polarity and the bonds' arrangement in the molecule.
CH3Cl carries polar bonds whose dipoles do not cancel, so the molecule is polar with the net dipole toward chlorine.
CCl4 carries four polar bonds whose dipoles cancel, so the molecule is nonpolar.

low.restatement: Each polar bond draws its own little arrow toward its negative end; add the arrows across the whole molecule - if they cancel, the molecule is neutral overall; if not, it is polar.
low.analogy: Four rowers pulling equally on a square raft keep it centred (CCl4); one rower pulling on one side sends it drifting (CH3Cl).
low.examPointer: Two-step answers score: bond polarities first, geometry second - never judge a molecule by bonds alone.

medium.restatement: Molecular polarity is the vector sum of bond dipoles: each bond contributes a moment pointing at its delta-negative end, and only symmetric arrangements - like CCl4's tetrahedron - let equal moments cancel to a nonpolar whole; asymmetric substitution like CH3Cl's single chlorine leaves a resultant moment.
medium.analogy: A mobile with balanced counterweights hangs level, but one off-centre ornament tilts the whole frame.
medium.examPointer: Quote the cancellation in words - the separate bond dipoles wipe each other away - that is the phrase the mark scheme wants.

glossary.definition: How strongly a bonded atom pulls the shared electron pair of its covalent bond toward itself.
The numbered scale on which electronegativity values are quoted, with fluorine highest at 4.0.
The measure of a bond's polarity, drawn as an arrow aimed at the delta-negative end.
Describing a bond or molecule whose charge centres coincide, leaving no separated partial charges.
